text: My body, my choice. Or should a man have a say in abortion? There are basically two ways people tend to look at this. One side says that pregnancy is happening in the woman's body, so ultimately it should be her decision. The other side says, well, it takes two people to create a child. Both the mother and the father are going to be parents, so both should have a say. And I understand both arguments, but there's an obvious problem with the second one. You can't really have a 50-50 decision here. You can't have half of a baby. If the woman wants an abortion and the man doesn't, or the man wants an abortion and the woman doesn't, somebody ultimately has to make that decision. So yes, I absolutely think the man should be able to express his concerns, explain what he wants, and have that conversation with the woman. But ultimately, because the pregnancy is happening in her body, I think the final decision has to be hers. Now, with that out of the way, here's where it gets more interesting. What happens if the man clearly says, I don't want to become a father, but the woman, who ultimately has the deciding vote, chooses to continue the pregnancy anyway? Should he still automatically be legally and financially responsible for that child? I don't think so. Again, in this video, I simply express my opinion and I do not claim to have the ultimate truth. But if the man clearly stated that he didn't want to become a father early enough, while abortion was still a legal and realistic option for the woman, I think he should have some ability to formally opt out of parenthood. Because think about what we just established. When the two people disagree, we ultimately take the decision out of his hands and give it to her. And I think there's a good reason for doing that. It is her body. But if she has the ultimate authority to make that decision, I don't think his own decision should suddenly become completely irrelevant when we start talking about the consequences. Especially if we're talking about a point in the pregnancy when abortion is still legally available to the woman. At that point, she knows he doesn't want to become a parent. She knows what the situation is and she's still making the decision to continue the pregnancy. Now, the obvious counter-argument is, okay, maybe the mother accepted that responsibility, but the child didn't. The child didn't choose to be born into that situation. And child support is supposed to support the child, not reward the mother. And I think that's actually a fair point. But I would say two things. First, the mother knew the circumstances when she made the decision. If she alone ultimately had the power to continue the pregnancy, then she also has to take some responsibility for the consequences of that decision. But second, I also don't think that should always mean that the child should get absolutely nothing from the biological father. So maybe there is a middle ground. If the father can show that during that early period he clearly and formally rejected becoming a parent, maybe he should still have to contribute some legally defined minimum amount necessary to support the child's basic needs. But that's it. It shouldn't suddenly become a percentage of his income or scale up massively because he later makes 100k, 500k, or 5 million a year. And obviously, if he opts out of the responsibilities, he also gives up the parental rights that come with them. To me, that seems like the fairest compromise. The woman keeps the final say over what happens to her body. The man's decision about becoming a parent isn't treated as completely meaningless. And once the child exists, the child still receives some basic level of support. What do you think?
